analysis.one_liner: Delays billion-dollar federal regulations until every court challenge against them is finished.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 244–180 on an almost purely party-line vote in September 2016, but the Senate never voted and it did not become law.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal agencies issue rules to carry out laws on things like air and water quality, workplace safety, and consumer finance. This bill says that any rule estimated to cost the economy $1 billion or more a year cannot take effect until every court challenge to it is completely resolved — or after 60 days if nobody sues. Because the companies those rules restrict are the ones with the money and lawyers to sue, the bill hands them a guaranteed delay, and a single lawsuit could freeze a major public protection for years while the case winds through court. It passed the House on a near-perfect party-line vote but never got a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Large companies facing rules that cost $1 billion or more a year — typically major energy, chemical, manufacturing, and financial firms. They get at least 60 extra days before any covered rule applies, and if they sue (which they are best positioned to do), the rule is frozen until the entire court case is finished, which can take years. A rule that is delayed past a change in administration can simply die.

how_it_helps.text: The bill postpones the effective date of any rule that the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs determines may cost the economy $1 billion or more a year until all court challenges to that rule are finally resolved [S3][S5].

Even if nobody sues, a covered rule cannot take effect until 60 days after publication (or after a longer review period if the underlying law provides one), giving regulated companies an automatic delay before compliance costs begin [S3][S5].
A final rule cannot even be published until the White House regulatory office (OIRA) classifies it as high-impact or not, adding a step before any billion-dollar rule reaches the public [S3][S5].
The bill also says courts may not be limited by law from issuing orders blocking a rule, underscoring that freezing rules through litigation is the bill's core mechanism [S5].

analysis.who_pays: The people the delayed rules were written to protect: workers, consumers, and communities waiting on safeguards for clean air and water, product safety, financial fraud, and similar protections. They bear the cost of the delay — exposure to hazards or unfair practices that continue while a company's lawsuit runs — and they get no offsetting benefit, since the review process already exists.

drawbacks.text: Any covered rule is frozen for as long as litigation lasts, and only one company has to sue to hold up a rule for years, even if the challenge is weak [S3][S5].
The delay applies to the rule itself, not just to the company suing, so everyone the rule protects — including people who support the rule — waits out the lawsuit [S5].

An honest supporter would concede the bill is not aimed at bad rules specifically: it covers every rule over the $1 billion cost threshold regardless of whether the rule is sound, trading the certainty of delay for whatever review it guarantees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated idea — making sure a court looks at very expensive rules before they take effect — has a surface appeal. But the design is one-sided: the parties most able to sue are the regulated companies, the delay is automatic and unlimited while litigation runs, and the entire cost of that delay falls on the people the rules protect. A rule costing $1 billion a year means the protections it delivers are also worth a great deal; freezing them for the two or three years a typical challenge takes is a real loss to the public with no matching gain. On balance, the bill is a delay tool for regulated industries more than a review safeguard.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House on a party-line vote in September 2016 but was referred to a Senate committee and never got a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 4, 2015 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which held a subcommittee hearing and reported it with amendments on September 13, 2016 [S7].
The House passed it on September 21, 2016 by a recorded vote of 244–180, with 240 of 245 Republicans voting yes and only 4 of 186 Democrats voting yes [S9].

Before the final vote, House Democrats offered a motion to send the bill back with instructions to add an exception for rules that reduce the public's vulnerability to terrorist attacks; it failed 182–240 along party lines [S7][S8].

The Senate received the bill on September 22, 2016 and referred it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee; no further action was taken before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5][S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who rely on federal protections are better off, because the bill never became law and major rules can take effect on their normal schedule. Companies that would have gained a guaranteed delay in billion-dollar rules did not get that tool.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public, since the bill never became law.

for.name: Rep. Tom Marino
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and managed it on the House floor, including demanding a recorded vote on a Democratic amendment.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a subcommittee hearing and reported the bill with amendments to the House floor on September 13, 2016.

for.name: House Rules Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the rule (H. Res. 875) that brought the bill to the floor for a vote on September 21, 2016.

against.name: Rep. Bennie Thompson
against.what_they_did: Moved to send the bill back to committee with instructions to add an exception for rules that reduce public vulnerability to terrorist attacks; the motion failed 182–240.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on September 22, 2016 and took no further action; the Senate never voted on it.

sides.party_line_note: On final passage, 240 of 245 Republicans voted yes and only 4 of 186 Democrats did; the motion to recommit split the same way, 0 Republicans for and 182 of 186 Democrats for.

industries.industry: Large regulated industries (major energy, chemical, manufacturing, and financial firms subject to $1 billion-a-year rules)
industries.note: These companies would get an automatic 60-day delay before any billion-dollar rule applies, and a single lawsuit by one of them would freeze the rule for the whole life of the case. The delay pushes off the compliance costs the rule exists to require, at the public's expense.

industries.industry: Law firms that litigate against federal rules on behalf of regulated companies
industries.note: By guaranteeing that any covered rule stays unenforced until court review is finished, the bill makes suing over a rule a near-guaranteed way to delay it, raising the value of challenges filed for regulated clients.
